questions.stem: A 48-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to his back and vomiting. Lipase is 7× the upper limit of normal. He is afebrile with BP 122/78 mmHg, HR 96/min, and SpO₂ 97% on room air. After initial IV fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer's, his pain is improving and he is tolerating sips of water. What is the most appropriate nutrition strategy?
options: A. Keep strictly NPO for at least 72 hours to rest the pancreas
B. Start early oral feeding as tolerated within 24 hours
C. Begin total parenteral nutrition immediately
D. Start clear liquids only after lipase normalizes
E. Initiate enteral feeds via nasojejunal tube regardless of tolerance
questions.rationale: Guidelines recommend early oral feeding as tolerated within 24 hours in acute pancreatitis, which improves outcomes compared with prolonged NPO. Prolonged fasting is no longer recommended, and parenteral nutrition is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate enteral routes. Lipase trends do not guide feeding decisions.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man hospitalized for pneumonia develops 7 watery stools over 18 hours on day 5 of ceftriaxone and azithromycin. He has a temperature of 38.4°C, WBC 16,200/µL, and creatinine that has risen from 1.0 to 1.5 mg/dL. He has no peritoneal signs. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
options: A. Give loperamide and observe for 48 hours
B. Start oral vancomycin and place contact enteric precautions while sending C. difficile testing
C. Order colonoscopy urgently to visualize pseudomembranes before starting any therapy
D. Send stool ova and parasite examination and defer antibiotics
E. Start empiric ciprofloxacin for bacterial gastroenteritis
questions.rationale: This presentation has high pretest probability for C. difficile infection given recent antibiotic exposure, fever, leukocytosis, and AKI. Prompt empiric therapy with oral vancomycin and contact enteric precautions are appropriate while testing is pending. Loperamide is contraindicated in suspected CDI due to risk of toxic megacolon. Colonoscopy is not needed before initiating treatment.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman is admitted for nausea, malaise, and jaundice. Labs show AST 2,800 U/L, ALT 3,200 U/L, total bilirubin 3.4 mg/dL, and INR 1.2. She is fully oriented with no asterixis. Which of the following tests should be ordered immediately regardless of the clinical suspicion?
options: A. Serum ceruloplasmin
B. Acetaminophen level
C. Hepatitis E IgM antibody
D. Anti-smooth muscle antibody
E. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
questions.rationale: An acetaminophen level should be sent in any case of acute hepatitis with marked transaminase elevation, even without a clear ingestion history, because acetaminophen toxicity is common, treatable with N-acetylcysteine, and easily missed when patients take combination products unknowingly. Delay in diagnosis worsens outcomes.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with no known liver disease presents with confusion and vomiting. Labs: AST 7,500 U/L, ALT 8,800 U/L, INR 2.6, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, glucose 52 mg/dL. She is somnolent but arousable. Which two findings together define acute liver failure?
options: A. Elevated transaminases and jaundice
B. Coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and hepatic encephalopathy without preexisting cirrhosis
C. Elevated bilirubin and ascites
D. Thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly
E. Elevated ammonia and asterixis
questions.rationale: Acute liver failure is defined by acute liver injury with coagulopathy (typically INR ≥1.5) and any degree of hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without known preexisting cirrhosis. Transaminase elevation alone or elevated ammonia without coagulopathy does not meet the definition. This distinction drives ICU-level management and early transplant-center involvement.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with gallstones presents with fever to 39.0°C, jaundice, and hypotension (BP 84/50 mmHg) after 1 L of crystalloid. Labs show WBC 20,000/µL, total bilirubin 7.2 mg/dL, and a dilated common bile duct on ultrasound. What is the most appropriate next step after starting antibiotics and resuscitation?
options: A. Schedule MRCP for the following morning to confirm choledocholithiasis
B. Arrange urgent biliary decompression via ERCP
C. Start corticosteroids for suspected autoimmune cholangitis
D. Obtain hepatitis serologies before any procedural intervention
E. Perform percutaneous liver biopsy to assess for granulomatous disease
questions.rationale: This presentation is severe acute cholangitis with shock and organ dysfunction, requiring urgent source control via biliary drainage (ERCP preferred) rather than confirmatory imaging that delays intervention. MRCP is appropriate for intermediate-risk, stable patients but should not delay drainage in unstable cholangitis.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with chronic diarrhea, bloating, and iron-deficiency anemia is admitted for evaluation. She is eating a normal diet containing wheat. Which initial diagnostic test strategy is most appropriate for suspected celiac disease?
options: A. HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping only
B. Tissue transglutaminase IgA (tTG-IgA) plus total IgA
C. Anti-saccharomyces cerevisiae antibodies (ASCA)
D. Stool calprotectin as the primary diagnostic test
E. Empiric gluten-free diet trial for 6 weeks before any testing
questions.rationale: First-line celiac screening in adults on a gluten-containing diet is tTG-IgA plus total IgA (to detect IgA deficiency that would invalidate IgA-based testing). HLA testing is mainly useful to rule out celiac when the patient is already gluten-free. Starting a gluten-free diet before testing reduces diagnostic sensitivity.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old immunocompetent man has had nonbloody watery diarrhea for 6 weeks with no weight loss, fever, or anemia. Basic metabolic panel and CBC are normal. According to AGA guidance, which single stool pathogen test is specifically recommended in this scenario?
options: A. Stool ova and parasite examination (three specimens)
B. Stool test for Giardia
C. Stool culture for Salmonella and Shigella
D. C. difficile PCR
E. Stool test for Cryptosporidium
questions.rationale: AGA guidance for chronic watery diarrhea without alarm features specifically recommends testing for Giardia, which is common and readily treatable. Routine broad ova and parasite testing without high-risk travel exposure is not recommended as initial workup, and bacterial cultures are targeted to acute presentations with inflammatory features.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents with hematemesis and melena. He is pale and tachycardic with HR 116/min and BP 90/54 mmHg. Hemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL. You suspect variceal hemorrhage. What hemoglobin range should be targeted with transfusion?
options: A. Hb ≥12 g/dL to ensure adequate oxygen delivery
B. Hb 7–9 g/dL using a restrictive transfusion strategy
C. Hb ≥10 g/dL in all patients with cirrhosis
D. No transfusion until endoscopy confirms the source
E. Transfuse only if systolic blood pressure falls below 70 mmHg
questions.rationale: Guidelines recommend a restrictive transfusion strategy targeting Hb 7–9 g/dL in acute variceal hemorrhage, as overtransfusion can worsen portal pressures and rebleeding. Liberal transfusion to Hb ≥10–12 is associated with worse outcomes in variceal bleeding.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man on the medicine floor develops 8 watery stools in 24 hours after completing a course of antibiotics. He is afebrile and hemodynamically stable. Labs show WBC 12,000/µL and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Stool testing confirms toxigenic C. difficile. What is the guideline-preferred initial treatment?
options: A. Metronidazole 500 mg PO TID for 10 days
B. Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID for 10 days
C. Vancomycin 500 mg PO QID for 14 days
D. Loperamide plus oral rehydration only
E. Fecal microbiota transplant as first-line therapy
questions.rationale: For an initial nonsevere CDI episode, IDSA/SHEA guidelines prefer fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID for 10 days, with oral vancomycin 125 mg QID as an acceptable alternative. Metronidazole is reserved as a fallback when preferred agents are unavailable. Antimotility agents are avoided due to toxic megacolon risk.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man with no family history of colorectal cancer and no GI symptoms asks about screening during a hospitalization for cellulitis. He has never been screened. What is the recommended screening interval for colonoscopy in an average-risk adult with a normal examination?
options: A. Every 3 years
B. Every 5 years
C. Every 10 years
D. Every 15 years
E. One-time colonoscopy with no repeat needed
questions.rationale: For average-risk adults choosing colonoscopy, the recommended screening interval after a normal, high-quality exam is every 10 years per major U.S. guidelines (USPSTF, ACG). Screening begins at age 45 for average-risk individuals.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man reports burning retrosternal discomfort and sour taste that worsen after meals and when lying flat. He has no dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, or odynophagia. Cardiac workup is negative. What is the best initial management?
options: A. Urgent upper endoscopy tonight
B. Barium swallow as the first diagnostic test
C. A proton pump inhibitor once daily 30–60 minutes before a meal for 8 weeks
D. Baclofen nightly for reflux symptoms
E. Surgical fundoplication referral
questions.rationale: For classic reflux symptoms without alarm features, guidelines recommend an empiric 8-week trial of a once-daily PPI taken 30–60 minutes before a meal. Endoscopy is prioritized for alarm symptoms such as dysphagia, GI bleeding, or weight loss, not for uncomplicated GERD.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with known cirrhosis is admitted for confusion and asterixis. He is afebrile and hemodynamically stable. He has not had a bowel movement in 3 days and recently started oxycodone after a fall. What is the best initial therapy for his altered mental status?
options: A. Rifaximin monotherapy
B. Lactulose titrated to 2–3 soft stools per day
C. Benzodiazepines for agitation
D. Dietary protein restriction to 0.6 g/kg/day
E. Flumazenil IV bolus
questions.rationale: Lactulose is the first-line treatment for episodic overt hepatic encephalopathy, titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day while precipitants (constipation, sedatives, dehydration) are corrected. Rifaximin is add-on therapy for recurrence prevention, typically after a second episode, not initial monotherapy. Protein restriction is not recommended.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is scheduled to start rituximab-based chemotherapy. Pre-treatment labs show: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative, total anti-HBc positive. ALT is normal. What is the best next step to reduce hepatitis-related complications?
options: A. No action needed; HBsAg is negative
B. Administer hepatitis B vaccine and proceed with chemotherapy
C. Begin entecavir prophylaxis before immunosuppression
D. Start sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for hepatitis prevention
E. Check HCV antibody only and proceed
questions.rationale: Anti-HBc positivity indicates prior HBV exposure and risk for reactivation with high-risk immunosuppression such as anti-CD20 therapy (rituximab). Guidelines favor prophylactic antiviral therapy (entecavir or tenofovir) over monitoring alone in this setting. Vaccination does not prevent reactivation from latent virus.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with known ulcerative colitis is admitted with 12 bloody stools per day, HR 106/min, T 38.1°C, and Hb 9.6 g/dL. C. difficile testing is negative. What is the standard IV corticosteroid regimen for acute severe ulcerative colitis?
options: A. Prednisone 10 mg PO daily
B. Methylprednisolone 60 mg IV daily
C. Budesonide 9 mg PO daily
D. Dexamethasone 40 mg IV daily for 4 days
E. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV daily
questions.rationale: For acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC), standard IV corticosteroid therapy is methylprednisolone 60 mg IV daily or hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q6h. Oral budesonide and low-dose oral prednisone are inadequate for ASUC. Response should be assessed objectively within 3–5 days.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with sudden large-volume hematochezia. He is tachycardic (HR 118/min) and hypotensive (BP 88/54 mmHg) despite 2 L of IV crystalloid. He continues to pass bright red blood. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step to localize the bleeding?
options: A. Urgent colonoscopy after rapid bowel preparation
B. Tagged red blood cell scintigraphy
C. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis
D. Capsule endoscopy
E. CT colonography
questions.rationale: In hemodynamically significant, ongoing lower GI bleeding, CT angiography rapidly localizes active bleeding and can guide interventional radiology embolization without delay for bowel preparation. CTA is the preferred rapid localization test when the patient is actively bleeding and unstable.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) develops sudden severe abdominal pain that is "10/10" and out of proportion to a soft, minimally tender abdomen. Lactate is 2.0 mmol/L. What is the best next diagnostic step?
options: A. Abdominal radiograph series and repeat exam in 4 hours
B. CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast immediately
C. Right upper quadrant ultrasound
D. Colonoscopy to evaluate for ischemic colitis
E. Serum lipase to rule out pancreatitis
questions.rationale: Acute mesenteric ischemia must be suspected when there is severe pain out of proportion to exam, especially with atrial fibrillation. CTA should be performed without delay as the first-line diagnostic test. Early lactate can be normal or only mildly elevated, so waiting for serial exams or plain radiographs risks catastrophic bowel infarction.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has had minimal oral intake for 10 days. A nasogastric tube is placed and continuous enteral feeding is ordered. His baseline labs show K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ 0.6 mmol/L, and phosphate 0.8 mmol/L. He is hemodynamically stable. What should be done before initiating feeds at the goal rate?
options: A. Start feeds at the goal rate and recheck electrolytes in 48 hours
B. Administer thiamine, replete electrolytes, and start feeds at a low rate with close monitoring
C. Hold all nutrition for 72 hours and give IV fluids only
D. Start an insulin infusion targeting glucose 80–110 mg/dL
E. Place a postpyloric tube before any feeding can begin
questions.rationale: This patient is at high risk for refeeding syndrome given prolonged poor intake and baseline electrolyte depletion. Thiamine must be given before or with feeding initiation, electrolytes aggressively repleted, and calories started low with close monitoring. Starting at goal rate risks life-threatening hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia, and respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man who takes naproxen daily presents with melena and lightheadedness. BP is 106/64 mmHg, HR 110/min. Hemoglobin is 7.4 g/dL, INR 1.0. After initial crystalloid resuscitation, what is the recommended timing for upper endoscopy in hospitalized upper GI bleeding?
options: A. Within 6 hours regardless of hemodynamic status
B. Within 24 hours after initial resuscitation
C. Within 72 hours to allow hemoglobin to stabilize
D. Only after hemoglobin is above 10 g/dL
E. Endoscopy is not needed if PPI therapy is started
questions.rationale: Guidelines recommend upper endoscopy within 24 hours of presentation for hospitalized UGIB after initial resuscitation. Routine ultra-early endoscopy (<6 hours) has not shown consistent benefit over timely endoscopy within 24 hours in hemodynamically stable patients. PPI therapy supports but does not replace endoscopic evaluation.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with known cirrhosis, ascites, and prior variceal banding presents with large-volume hematemesis. BP is 86/50 mmHg, HR 126/min. While blood products are being prepared, which two medication classes should be started immediately?
options: A. PPI and antiemetic
B. Vasoactive agent (octreotide) and antibiotic (ceftriaxone)
C. Anticoagulant and antiplatelet
D. Corticosteroid and prokinetic
E. H2 blocker and sucralfate
questions.rationale: In suspected acute variceal hemorrhage, immediate management includes a vasoactive agent (e.g., octreotide bolus then infusion) plus antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g., ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily). These reduce rebleeding and infection risk and should not be delayed for endoscopic confirmation of varices.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man with decompensated cirrhosis and ascites is admitted overnight with fever and diffuse abdominal tenderness. Paracentesis shows 1,400 WBC/µL with 82% neutrophils; cultures are pending. What ascitic PMN threshold defines SBP and triggers empiric antibiotics?
options: A. ≥100 cells/µL
B. ≥250 cells/µL
C. ≥500 cells/µL
D. ≥1,000 cells/µL
E. Only after positive culture
questions.rationale: SBP is diagnosed by an ascitic absolute neutrophil count ≥250 cells/µL, and empiric antibiotics should be started at or above this threshold regardless of culture results. Waiting for culture confirmation delays life-saving treatment. Culture-negative neutrocytic ascites is treated the same as culture-positive SBP.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with HFrEF (EF 25%) is admitted with acute pancreatitis (lipase 5× ULN). BP is 90/56 mmHg, HR 120/min, SpO₂ 89% on 4 L/min nasal cannula with bibasilar crackles. She received 2 L of lactated Ringer's in the ED. BUN is rising and urine output is low. What is the best next step?
options: A. Continue aggressive fluid boluses until urine output normalizes
B. Start prophylactic antibiotics for suspected severe pancreatitis
C. Initiate ICU-level, goal-directed resuscitation with careful titration and early vasopressors if MAP remains <65 mmHg
D. Order immediate contrast CT to assess necrosis extent
E. Start parenteral nutrition immediately to prevent catabolism
questions.rationale: The key pitfall is over-resuscitating a patient with limited cardiac reserve. Guidelines support goal-directed fluids with frequent reassessment, escalating to ICU care and vasopressors when shock evolves in patients with cardiovascular comorbidity. Continued large boluses in a patient with crackles and low EF will worsen pulmonary edema. Routine early CT and prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman admitted for cellulitis develops sudden severe crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea after eating a hamburger brought from home. T 38.0°C, BP 120/76 mmHg, HR 102/min. She has diffuse tenderness without guarding. The team plans empiric azithromycin and loperamide. What is the best alternative approach?
options: A. Start azithromycin and give loperamide for symptom control as planned
B. Send stool testing for Shiga toxin–producing organisms and provide supportive care without antibiotics or antimotility agents
C. Start high-dose oral vancomycin for presumed C. difficile
D. Administer prednisone for presumed IBD flare
E. Give bismuth subsalicylate and discharge
questions.rationale: Bloody diarrhea with severe cramps after ground beef exposure raises high concern for STEC (Shiga toxin–producing E. coli). Guidelines caution against empiric antibiotics in suspected STEC due to potential increased risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome. Antimotility agents are also avoided in inflammatory diarrhea. The pitfall is reflexively treating bloody diarrhea with antibiotics without considering STEC.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman on chronic warfarin for atrial fibrillation is admitted with abdominal discomfort and dark urine. AST 1,050 U/L, ALT 1,200 U/L, bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL, INR 3.2. She is fully oriented with normal mental status and no asterixis. She took her usual warfarin dose today. What is the best approach to determine whether she has acute liver failure?
options: A. Diagnose acute liver failure based on INR alone and arrange emergent transfer
B. Attribute INR entirely to warfarin and ignore hepatic synthetic function
C. Assess for encephalopathy and interpret INR in context; trend INR off warfarin and check additional synthesis markers
D. Give fresh frozen plasma to normalize INR and repeat liver enzymes in the morning
E. Start lactulose immediately because any INR elevation implies hepatic encephalopathy
questions.rationale: Warfarin elevates INR independent of liver synthetic function, creating a diagnostic pitfall. Acute liver failure requires both coagulopathy from hepatic dysfunction and encephalopathy. The correct approach is to assess mental status carefully, hold warfarin and trend INR, and consider additional markers of hepatic synthesis (e.g., factor V, fibrinogen) rather than reflexively diagnosing or dismissing ALF.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with acute liver failure from suspected drug-induced injury is intubated for encephalopathy in the ICU. Labs: INR 3.4, platelets 30 × 10⁹/L, fibrinogen 1.5 g/L. He has no active bleeding. The team asks whether pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis should be given since 'his INR is so high he can't clot.' What is the best prophylaxis approach?
options: A. Enoxaparin 40 mg SC nightly
B. Unfractionated heparin 5,000 units SC every 8 hours
C. No prophylaxis needed because elevated INR means auto-anticoagulation
D. Mechanical prophylaxis with sequential compression devices only
E. Give fresh frozen plasma first, then start enoxaparin
questions.rationale: A common pitfall is assuming elevated INR in ALF means the patient is 'auto-anticoagulated' — ALF patients have rebalanced hemostasis and can still develop thrombosis. However, with platelets at 30 × 10⁹/L, pharmacologic prophylaxis carries significant bleeding risk. Mechanical prophylaxis is preferred here while platelet counts and bleeding risk are reassessed. Correcting INR with plasma solely to enable heparin is not recommended without active bleeding.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman is admitted for RUQ pain. She is afebrile with stable vitals. Labs show AST 220 U/L, ALT 270 U/L, ALP 195 U/L, bilirubin 2.9 mg/dL. Ultrasound shows gallstones and CBD diameter of 7 mm with no visible stone. She has a history of post-ERCP pancreatitis. What is the best diagnostic approach?
options: A. Proceed directly to ERCP tonight
B. Obtain MRCP or EUS to confirm choledocholithiasis before ERCP
C. Start antibiotics and schedule cholecystectomy only
D. Start heparin infusion for suspected hepatic vein thrombosis
E. Repeat ultrasound in 48 hours and observe
questions.rationale: This is intermediate-risk suspected choledocholithiasis (abnormal liver tests and mildly dilated CBD without high-risk criteria like bilirubin >4 or visible stone). Noninvasive confirmation with MRCP or EUS is preferred to avoid unnecessary ERCP, which is especially important given her history of post-ERCP pancreatitis. Direct ERCP is reserved for high-risk presentations or confirmed cholangitis.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old patient with chronic diarrhea and iron-deficiency anemia self-started a gluten-free diet 3 months ago with partial improvement. They are now admitted for syncope with orthostatic hypotension. You need to determine whether they truly have celiac disease. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
options: A. Order tTG-IgA only
B. Order HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping
C. Start oral budesonide for presumed refractory celiac disease
D. Diagnose celiac disease based on symptom improvement alone
E. Order duodenal biopsies immediately without considering diet status
questions.rationale: When a patient has already eliminated gluten, serology and biopsy may normalize and become unreliable. In this setting, HLA-DQ2/DQ8 negativity effectively rules out celiac disease, while positivity is nondiagnostic but may prompt a supervised gluten challenge. The pitfall is assuming symptom improvement on a GFD confirms the diagnosis — many conditions improve with dietary modification.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman hospitalized for atrial fibrillation has had 3 months of chronic watery diarrhea including nocturnal episodes. She takes a PPI and ibuprofen daily. A colonoscopy 2 weeks ago showed completely normal-appearing mucosa. Labs are normal. What is the best next step to establish the diagnosis?
options: A. Reassure her that a normal colonoscopy rules out colitis
B. Start loperamide as first-line therapy
C. Obtain random colonic biopsies to evaluate for microscopic colitis
D. Order ESR and CRP to screen for IBD
E. Start empiric oral vancomycin for presumed C. difficile
questions.rationale: The classic pitfall is assuming a normal-appearing colon excludes microscopic colitis. Microscopic colitis presents with chronic watery diarrhea (often nocturnal) and a grossly normal colon — diagnosis requires colonic biopsies. PPI and NSAID exposure increases suspicion. Treatment with budesonide is effective once confirmed.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis is found overnight to be progressively somnolent and confused with asterixis. She is intermittently vomiting. Vitals are stable and SpO₂ is 94% on room air. The nurse asks for lactulose now. What is the best next step?
options: A. Administer lactulose orally immediately
B. Place an NG tube and give lactulose without further evaluation
C. Secure the airway first, then administer enteral lactulose targeting 2–3 soft stools/day
D. Give IV benzodiazepines for agitation and reassess in 2 hours
E. Order screening endoscopy before treating encephalopathy
questions.rationale: The immediate pitfall is aspiration risk — this patient has depressed mental status and active emesis. Airway protection must come first. Once the airway is secured, lactulose can be safely administered targeting 2–3 soft stools/day. Giving oral lactulose to a vomiting, somnolent patient without airway assessment risks aspiration. Benzodiazepines worsen encephalopathy.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with CKD (baseline Cr 2.0 mg/dL) is admitted with abdominal pain and confusion. She has minimal stool output with nausea, distention, and diffuse tenderness. T 38.3°C, BP 84/52 mmHg after 2 L crystalloid, HR 118/min. WBC 28,000/µL, lactate 4.1 mmol/L. CT shows diffuse colitis with colonic dilation and ileus concern. Which antimicrobial regimen is best?
options: A. Fidaxomicin 200 mg PO BID only
B. Vancomycin 125 mg PO QID only
C. Vancomycin 500 mg PO/NG Q6H plus metronidazole 500 mg IV Q8H, plus vancomycin 500 mg PR Q6H
D. Metronidazole 500 mg PO TID only
E. Defer CDI therapy until stool testing confirms diagnosis
questions.rationale: This is fulminant CDI with shock, ileus, and megacolon concern. Fulminant disease requires high-dose enteral vancomycin (500 mg Q6H) plus IV metronidazole. The critical pitfall is ileus preventing adequate colonic drug delivery — rectal vancomycin must be added. Standard doses and single-agent regimens are inadequate. Waiting for confirmatory testing risks fatal deterioration.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman is hospitalized for an asthma exacerbation. She reports her father was diagnosed with colon cancer at age 50. She has no GI symptoms and has never been screened. What is the most appropriate colorectal cancer screening recommendation?
options: A. Begin screening at age 45 with annual FIT
B. Begin screening now with colonoscopy and repeat every 10 years if normal
C. Begin screening now with colonoscopy and repeat every 5 years if normal
D. Begin screening at age 50 with colonoscopy every 10 years
E. No screening indicated because she is asymptomatic
questions.rationale: A first-degree relative with CRC diagnosed before age 60 places her in a higher-risk category. Screening should begin at age 40 or 10 years before the youngest family diagnosis (whichever is earlier), using colonoscopy with 5-year intervals if normal. The pitfall is applying average-risk guidelines (start at 45, 10-year intervals) to a patient with significant family history.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman on alendronate is admitted for cellulitis. At 2 AM she develops sudden severe odynophagia and substernal pain after taking her bedtime pills with a small sip of water while lying flat. She is afebrile, hemodynamically stable, with no drooling or respiratory distress. What is the best next step?
options: A. Give a large oral water challenge to push the pills through
B. Keep NPO, start PPI, provide analgesia, and stop the offending medication
C. Start IV thrombolytics for presumed esophageal ischemia
D. Place a nasogastric tube for decompression
E. Start high-dose oral steroids immediately
questions.rationale: This presentation is classic pill esophagitis from alendronate taken with insufficient water in a recumbent position. Management is stopping the offending agent, reducing acid exposure with PPI, and supportive care. The pitfall is forcing oral intake that may worsen mucosal injury, or blind instrumentation (NG tube) without indication. Bisphosphonates are a well-known cause of pill esophagitis.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis is brought in for acute confusion. She is somnolent but arousable, has no asterixis, and her family says 'this looks like her prior hepatic encephalopathy.' Vitals are stable and she is afebrile. Her plasma ammonia level returns normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Stop further evaluation because normal ammonia excludes HE
B. Treat with lactulose only and defer all other workup
C. Re-evaluate for alternative causes of encephalopathy with targeted testing
D. Start high-dose protein restriction immediately
E. Start rifaximin as monotherapy for presumed covert HE
questions.rationale: A normal ammonia level calls the diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy into question and should prompt re-evaluation for alternative causes (infection, metabolic derangements, stroke, intoxication). The pitfall is anchoring on the cirrhosis history and skipping the standard encephalopathy workup. Elevated ammonia doesn't confirm HE, but normal ammonia should shift the differential.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is admitted for respiratory failure. The team plans prednisone 60 mg daily with a slow taper over months. HBV labs return: HBsAg positive, anti-HBs negative, anti-HBc positive. ALT is 78 U/L. HBV DNA is pending. What is the best next step?
options: A. Start tenofovir or entecavir now while steroids begin
B. Delay steroids until HBV DNA results return
C. Give hepatitis B vaccine now and reassess in 1 month
D. Start ribavirin to prevent flare
E. Monitor ALT weekly and start antivirals only if ALT exceeds 200 U/L
questions.rationale: HBsAg positivity indicates chronic HBV, and high-dose prolonged steroids can precipitate severe reactivation/flares. A high-barrier antiviral should be started promptly when significant immunosuppression is initiated. The pitfall is waiting for DNA levels when the trigger (steroids) is imminent and HBsAg is already positive — prophylaxis should not be delayed.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis on azathioprine presents with 6 days of worsening watery diarrhea and new hematochezia. HR 112/min, T 38.0°C. CT shows diffuse colitis without perforation. Stool testing returns positive for C. difficile. The team plans to start IV methylprednisolone for ASUC. What is the best next step?
options: A. Start methylprednisolone 60 mg IV daily immediately
B. Start oral vancomycin 125 mg q6h and hold escalation of immunosuppression until infection is addressed
C. Start infliximab as rescue therapy tonight
D. Start loperamide and oral rehydration only
E. Perform colonoscopy with full bowel prep overnight
questions.rationale: The critical pitfall is treating an infectious colitis mimic as an IBD flare. A positive C. difficile test shifts first-line management to targeted antibiotic therapy before escalating immunosuppression. CDI is a common trigger for worsening symptoms in IBD patients and must be addressed first. Escalating steroids or biologics with untreated CDI can worsen outcomes.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with hematochezia and lightheadedness. She is diaphoretic with HR 130/min and BP 80/46 mmHg. She has a history of peptic ulcer disease and took ibuprofen daily. She has no abdominal pain. After initiating transfusion and resuscitation, what is the best next procedure?
options: A. Colonoscopy as soon as bowel prep is complete
B. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (upper endoscopy)
C. Capsule endoscopy
D. CT colonography
E. No endoscopy; observe with IV fluids only
questions.rationale: The key pitfall is assuming hematochezia always means a lower GI source. Hematochezia with hemodynamic instability can represent a brisk upper GI bleed with rapid transit, especially in a patient with PUD history and NSAID use. Upper endoscopy should be performed first to exclude a treatable upper source before pursuing colonic evaluation.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with diffuse atherosclerosis presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and vomiting. BP is 90/52 mmHg, HR 120/min. Creatinine is 3.4 mg/dL (baseline unknown). Lactate is 4.0 mmol/L. The team hesitates to order contrast imaging because of acute kidney injury. What is the best next step?
options: A. Obtain noncontrast CT first and reassess
B. Obtain CT angiography with IV contrast immediately while resuscitating
C. Start total parenteral nutrition and observe overnight
D. Treat empirically for pancreatitis and recheck lipase
E. Perform colonoscopy to evaluate for ischemic colitis
questions.rationale: The pitfall is delaying definitive diagnosis for renal concerns in a life-threatening emergency. CTA should not be delayed when clinical suspicion for acute mesenteric ischemia is high, even with AKI, because rapid vascular imaging drives reperfusion decisions that determine survival. The risk of missing AMI far outweighs contrast nephropathy risk in this scenario.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with septic shock is in the ICU on norepinephrine at 0.25 µg/kg/min with rising lactate and cool extremities. A new order is placed to start continuous enteral feeds overnight because she has been NPO for 2 days. Her abdomen is soft but mildly distended. What is the best next step?
options: A. Start full-rate gastric feeds now to prevent gut mucosal atrophy
B. Start trophic feeds and advance every 2 hours regardless of pressor dose
C. Hold enteral feeds until she is adequately resuscitated and vasopressor requirements are stable or decreasing
D. Switch to bolus feeds to improve tolerance
E. Place a postpyloric tube and start full-rate feeds immediately
questions.rationale: Enteral feeding should be withheld during active hemodynamic instability (escalating vasopressors, rising lactate, poor perfusion) due to risk of gut ischemia. The pitfall is assuming 'some feeds are always safe' during shock. Cautious initiation may be considered once pressors are stable or de-escalating, with close monitoring.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman with prior MI takes aspirin 81 mg daily for secondary prevention. She develops hematemesis and melena. After resuscitation, endoscopy shows a bleeding duodenal ulcer that is successfully treated. Which antiplatelet plan is most appropriate?
options: A. Stop aspirin indefinitely because it caused the ulcer
B. Hold aspirin for at least 30 days to prevent rebleeding
C. Resume aspirin as soon as possible after hemostasis for secondary cardiovascular prevention
D. Switch to clopidogrel immediately without PPI co-therapy
E. Start therapeutic heparin bridging while aspirin is held
questions.rationale: The pitfall is over-holding antiplatelet therapy in secondary prevention. Guidelines support continuing or early resumption of low-dose aspirin after endoscopic hemostasis because the cardiovascular risk of interruption is significant. PPI co-therapy is standard after ulcer bleeding. Bridging anticoagulation is not indicated for aspirin interruption.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with known cirrhosis presents with large-volume hematemesis. BP is 86/50 mmHg, HR 126/min, and he is intermittently confused. Hemoglobin is 7.8 g/dL, INR 1.9, platelets 76 × 10⁹/L. While blood is being prepared, the team suggests correcting the INR with fresh frozen plasma before starting any other therapy. What is the best immediate intervention?
options: A. Give 4 units FFP to correct INR before starting octreotide
B. Start octreotide infusion plus ceftriaxone immediately
C. Give vitamin K 10 mg IV and wait for INR correction
D. Administer desmopressin for platelet dysfunction
E. Start tranexamic acid infusion as first-line therapy
questions.rationale: The pitfall is focusing on INR correction in variceal bleeding. Routine correction of mildly abnormal INR in cirrhosis does not address the portal pressure–driven hemorrhage and delays definitive management. Vasoactive therapy (octreotide) plus antibiotic prophylaxis (ceftriaxone) should begin immediately alongside resuscitation. Tranexamic acid has not shown benefit in GI bleeding.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with decompensated cirrhosis and recurrent SBP is admitted from a skilled nursing facility with fever and abdominal discomfort. She has been taking norfloxacin prophylaxis for months. BP is 94/56 mmHg after 1 L crystalloid, HR 114/min. Paracentesis shows ascitic PMN 580 cells/µL. Which empiric antibiotic approach is most appropriate?
options: A. Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h as standard community-acquired SBP therapy
B. Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg BID
C. Piperacillin-tazobactam IV with de-escalation when cultures return
D. Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole only
E. Defer antibiotics until culture identifies the organism
questions.rationale: This is healthcare-associated SBP with quinolone prophylaxis, increasing the likelihood of resistant organisms and potential failure of standard third-generation cephalosporin therapy. The pitfall is applying community-acquired coverage to a patient with MDRO risk factors. Broader empiric therapy with prompt de-escalation based on cultures is favored when severity and exposure history suggest resistance.
